title: Given a collection of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort intervals by start, then sweep left to right: extend the current interval when the next overlaps, otherwise close it and begin a new one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Merge intervals** – combine any intervals that overlap or touch into single continuous intervals, producing a minimal non-overlapping set.
- **Sort by start** – sorting makes overlap detection local; after sorting, any overlapping interval must overlap the most recently merged one.
- **Extend current end** – when the next interval's start is at or before the current end, merge by taking the maximum of the two ends.
- **Max-end rule** – taking the maximum handles the case where the next interval is fully contained within the current one.
- **Flush final** – after the loop, push the last current interval to the result because it is only closed by a gap that may never come.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has many maintenance windows on the core system throughout a day, some overlapping. He lines them up by start time and sweeps once: if the next window starts before the current block ends, they merge into one outage period. If there is a gap, he finalises the current block and starts a new one. The finalised blocks are the real outage periods shown to customers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
     Merge Intervals: Sort + Sweep

     Input:  [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] [15,18]
     Sorted: [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] [15,18]  (already sorted)

     Step 1: current = [1,3]
     Step 2: [2,6] start=2 <= 3=end => merge, end=max(3,6)=6
             current = [1,6]
     Step 3: [8,10] start=8 > 6=end => gap!
             result: [1,6]
             current = [8,10]
     Step 4: [15,18] start=15 > 10=end => gap!
             result: [1,6], [8,10]
             current = [15,18]
     Flush:  result: [1,6], [8,10], [15,18]

     Containment example:
     ┌──────────────┐
     │   [1, 10]    │  current
     │  ┌──────┐    │
     │  │[2, 5]│    │  next (fully contained)
     │  └──────┘    │
     └──────────────┘
     max(10, 5) = 10 => current stays [1, 10]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging intervals sorts the input by start time and sweeps once, extending the current interval when the next overlaps and starting a new one when there is a gap. Sorting makes overlap detection local: once intervals are in start order, any overlap must involve the most recently merged interval, so the sweep is a single linear pass.

The two correctness traps are the max-end rule and the final flush. When merging, always take the maximum of the current end and the next end, because the next interval might be fully contained and the current end must not shrink. After the loop, always push the current interval to the result, because it is only closed by a gap that may never come.

The touching policy is a domain decision. For maintenance windows at National Bank of India, touching windows form a continuous outage, so Rajesh uses less-than-or-equal for the overlap test. For booking slots where back-to-back use is allowed, strict less-than keeps them separate.

This is the base template for the entire merge-intervals family. Insert Interval, Interval Intersection, Meeting Rooms, and free-gap computation all build on the sort-and-sweep skeleton. Mastering this one unlocks a whole family of interval questions, and a senior engineer recognises it as a pattern rather than a one-off.

Remember one sentence: sort by start, sweep left to right extending the current interval on overlap with max-end, and always flush the final interval after the loop.

---

keyPoints: Sort intervals by start time to make overlap detection local: only compare with the most recently merged interval.
When overlapping, extend the current end to Math.max(currentEnd, nextEnd) to handle containment correctly.
After the loop, always push the final current interval to the result to avoid the off-by-one bug.
Use <= for the overlap test when touching intervals should merge (continuous blocks), < when they should not.
Time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the sweep; space is O(n) for the result.
This is the base template for the entire merge-intervals family: insert, intersect, meeting rooms, free gaps.
